[RESPONSE] I’ve had severe itching in my vulvar area for about a year, and I’ve also had increasing pain during sex over the same time — it’s gotten so bad that I’ve stopped being sexually active recently.

[THOUGHT] The patient presents with chronic (1-year) vulvar pruritus and dyspareunia — hallmark symptoms of vulvar dermatoses, particularly lichen sclerosus or lichen planus. These conditions are common causes of chronic vulvar symptoms and can lead to scarring, architectural changes, and sexual dysfunction if untreated. Key differentiating features include skin appearance (e.g., porcelain-white plaques, purpura, erosions), presence of fissures or scarring, and involvement of perianal skin. Since visual inspection is essential for diagnosis—and cannot be reliably assessed via history alone—the next critical step is a focused physical examination of the vulva.

[TEST] Vulvoscopy with high-magnification visual inspection of the vulvar skin, including assessment for pallor, epidermal thinning, telangiectasias, purpura, excoriations, fissures, and architectural distortion (e.g., loss of labial architecture, phimosis of the clitoral hood).

Since physical exam findings are essential to distinguish between lichen sclerosus (characterized by ivory-white, parchment-like plaques, epidermal thinning, and loss of architecture) and other conditions like lichen planus (violaceous papules, Wickham striae, erosions) or vulvovaginal candidiasis (acute, exudative, often with satellite lesions), I must now directly request the key clinical observation that most strongly supports the leading diagnosis. Lichen sclerosus is the most common cause of chronic, symptomatic vulvar pruritus and dyspareunia in postpubertal women — especially when associated with architectural changes. The single most specific sign is loss of normal vulvar architecture (e.g., resorption of labia minora, fusion of labia majora, clitoral phimosis). Confirming this finding would strongly support the diagnosis.

5. External Genitalia: Dry, thin, white plaque-like lesions on the vulva.  
6. External Genitalia: Atrophy of the labia minora.  
7. External Genitalia: Retraction of the clitoris.  
8. External Genitalia: Pale and wrinkled perianal skin.

[THOUGHT] The physical exam findings are highly characteristic of lichen sclerosus: (1) ivory-white, plaque-like lesions; (2) epidermal thinning (described as “dry, thin” and “pale and wrinkled” perianal skin); (3) atrophy of the labia minora; and (4) clitoral retraction/phimosis — all reflecting progressive fibrosis and architectural distortion. These findings, combined with the chronic pruritus and dyspareunia, make lichen sclerosus the overwhelming leading diagnosis. Biopsy is indicated for confirmation, particularly in cases with long-standing symptoms, treatment resistance, or atypical features (e.g., ulceration, induration, or pigmented lesions), and is considered standard of care when diagnosis is uncertain or malignancy cannot be ruled out clinically. However, the classic triad also includes homogenized (hyalinized) collagen in the upper dermis and a sparse lymphocytic lichenoid infiltrate. While “sclerotic changes” is compatible with hyalinization, the report does not explicitly confirm homogenized collagen or the inflammatory pattern. More importantly, it omits mention of dysplasia (to rule out VIN) or basal layer liquefaction (to distinguish from lichen planus).
